prompt:
Moral Foundations Theory is a framework that separates human morality into the following categories:

  - Care/Harm: related to our long evolution as mammals with attachment systems
    and an ability to feel (and dislike) the pain of others. It underlies the
    virtues of kindness, gentleness, and nurturance.

  - Loyalty/Betrayal: related to our long history as tribal creatures able to
    form shifting coalitions. It is active anytime people feel that it is "one
    for all and all for one." It underlies the virtues of patriotism and
    self-sacrifice for the group.

  - Authority/Subversion: shaped by our long primate history of hierarchical
    social interactions. It underlies virtues of leadership and followership,
    including deference to prestigious authority figures and respect for
    traditions.

  - Sanctity/Purity: shaped by the psychology of disgust and contamination. It
    underlies notions of striving to live in an elevated, less carnal, more
    noble, and more "natural" way (often present in religious narratives). This
    foundation underlies the widespread idea that the body is a temple that can
    be desecrated by immoral activities and contaminants (an idea not unique to
    religious traditions). It underlies the virtues of self-discipline,
    self-improvement, naturalness, and spirituality.

  - Equality: related to our intuitions about equal treatment and equal outcome
    for individuals.

  - Proportionality: related to our intuitions about individuals getting
    rewarded in proportion to their merit or contribution.

Every category has a bidirectional nature. For example:

One person's sensitivity to the Care/Harm foundation may lead them to support high levels of immigration from poorer nations, to reduce the suffering of those who migrate. Whereas another person's sensitivity to the very same foundation may lead them to oppose those levels, because they believe it could lead to people they care about being harmed.

TEXT_E:
Britain forward, not back. New Labour’s 2005 manifesto applies enduring Labour values to a changing world with one core duty: government must provide opportunity and security for all. It seeks to embed a progressive consensus that rejects the old false choices between wealth creation and social justice, security and liberty, equal rights and protection from crime. The offer is investment plus reform; rights matched by responsibilities; services free to all, personal to each.

Record: macroeconomic stability, record employment, low inflation and mortgage rates; tax credits and a minimum wage that make work pay; real-terms investment transforming schools and the NHS; crime down 30%; poverty reduced for children and pensioners; stronger leadership in Europe; doubled aid and first-in-class action on climate through emissions trading.

Economy: entrench low debt and high employment under strict fiscal rules and a 2% inflation target; no rise in basic or top income tax rates, no VAT on essentials; redirect £21bn efficiencies to the frontline. Build an “opportunity economy” with skills, science (R&D to 2.5% of GDP by 2014), support for manufacturing and SMEs, fair procurement, lighter, smarter regulation, and competitive capital markets. Aim for 80% employment via New Deal, higher minimum wage, incapacity benefit reform, and personalised back-to-work support. Invest over £180bn in transport to 2015, with better rail, potential high-speed links, bus concessions, safety and low-carbon innovation, while exploring fair road pricing. Spread prosperity to every region; strengthen equality at work; back thriving rural economies and environmental stewardship.

Education: personalised learning and parental partnership from early years to HE. More teachers and support staff; primary basics plus arts, sport and languages; every secondary an independent specialist school, with fair admissions, strong discipline, and 200 Academies by 2010; Building Schools for the Future for modern facilities; stretch for the brightest and targeted catch-up. Transform 14–19 with high-quality vocational routes, specialised diplomas, apprenticeships and EMAs; reform FE; expand HE with fair, capped variable fees, bursaries and grants, and a 50% participation aim.

Crime and security: neighbourhood policing teams in every community; firm action on antisocial behaviour and alcohol-related disorder; tackle drugs with compulsory testing and treatment; create the Serious Organised Crime Agency; tougher penalties on guns and knives; cut reoffending with end-to-end offender management; strengthen victims’ rights. Managed migration that benefits Britain: a points-based system favouring skills, secure borders with biometrics and ID cards, faster, fairer asylum. Tackle terrorism with robust laws while upholding liberties.

NHS: free to all, personal to each; no charges for operations. Triple spending by 2008; cut referral-to-treatment waits to 18 weeks; expand capacity via NHS, independent and voluntary providers meeting NHS standards; extend patient choice; shift care to primary and community settings, including new community hospitals; drive cleanliness and clinical governance; focus on prevention—healthier school meals, food labelling, smoke-free workplaces and expanded cessation services.

Older people and families: maintain Pension Credit and universal benefits; build a cross-party pensions settlement that rewards saving; flexible retirement and work beyond 65; individual care budgets. End child poverty in a generation with tax credits, a Child Trust Fund, universal early years, 3,500 Sure Start Children’s Centres, extended schools 8–6, more paid maternity leave and flexible working; boost homeownership and renew social housing with more choice.

International: a leading Britain in a reformed EU; constitutional treaty by referendum; NATO at the core of defence; modern, well-equipped armed forces and a retained independent nuclear deterrent; support for democracy in Iraq and the Middle East; UN, World Bank and IMF reform. Global leadership on climate change (−20% CO2 by 2010, −60% by 2050) and on Africa (0.7% ODA by 2013, debt relief, fairer trade, universal access to AIDS treatment and basic services).

Quality of life and democracy: culture and sport for all (free museums, facilities, Olympic legacy); digital switchover; cleaner neighbourhoods, greener planning, a Marine Act. Devolution deepened; stronger, more accountable local government and neighbourhood powers; complete Lords reform; a Single Equality Act and a new Commission on Equality and Human Rights. The social contract remains clear: we help you; you help yourself; we all move forward together.

TEXT_C:
The Green Party’s 2005 manifesto sets out a realistic, values-driven programme for social, economic and environmental justice—putting people and planet before short-term profit, reversing privatisation, tackling inequality, and confronting climate change. It champions democracy, peace and localisation to build shared prosperity and long-term security.

- Economics: Tackle inequality with more progressive income tax bands, higher Corporation Tax for large firms, a progressive inheritance tax on recipients, and abolition of National Insurance in favour of broader income taxation. Pilot a Land Value Tax to replace Council Tax and Uniform Business Rates. Replace VAT with revenue‑neutral eco‑taxes that price resource use, waste and pollution. Back small firms, co‑ops and community banks; promote credit unions and local currencies; oppose UK entry to the euro; reform global trade rules. Create green jobs and defend workers’ rights; measure real progress beyond GDP.

- Energy and climate: Adopt Contraction and Convergence, cutting UK CO2 by 20% by 2010 on a path to 85% by 2030. Replace VAT/CCL on energy with a Carbon Tax, protecting low users. Reach 40% renewables by 2020 through major investment in wind, solar, wave and biogas, and shift R&D from nuclear to renewables. Cut demand via a Warmer Homes Act and Smart Energy Councils. Decommission nuclear as stations reach end of life.

- Welfare: Phase in a universal, non‑withdrawable Citizen’s Income to replace most means‑tested benefits; retain and then integrate housing benefit; keep disability/incapacity benefits additional. Establish a universal Citizen’s Pension linked to earnings, replacing Pension Credit. Support families by simplifying child support, raising Child Benefit, reducing working hours, and expanding Sure Start. Boost affordable housing through council building, self‑build co‑ops, LVT, and energy efficiency.

- Health and education: Restore the NHS to universal, comprehensive, publicly provided care; end PFI/PPP and foundation hospitals; oppose GATS in public services. Abolish prescription, eye test and dental charges; expand access to holistic care. Raise health spending to at least 9% of GNP, with a hypothecated NHS tax. In education, fund lifelong learning, expand pre‑school, scrap tuition fees and restore maintenance grants; abolish SATs and move toward Individual Learning Plans.

- Transport: Prioritise walking, cycling and public transport; cut road traffic 10% by 2010; re‑regulate buses; return rail and tube to public ownership; expand rail and light rail. Reflect true costs of motoring via congestion/road pricing, higher fuel duty and freight levies; invest in clean vehicle R&D. Resist airport expansion, ban night flights, and tax aviation fuel/emissions.

- Environment: Commit to Zero Waste with a ban on incineration, a national agency, and 60% recycling by 2010. Levy eco‑taxes on polluting inputs; create an Environmental Protection Commission. Apply the precautionary principle to GM, xenotransplantation and nanotech; oppose patents on genetic resources; strengthen animal welfare (end live exports, ban battery eggs, curb fur; replace vivisection).

- Food and farming: Pass an Organics Target Bill (30% by 2012); replace CAP/CFP with support for organic, local and biodiversity‑enhancing systems; ban GM food; curb supermarket market power.

- Crime and justice: Prevent crime by strengthening communities—better urban design, youth facilities, rapid repairs, treating drugs as a health issue; oppose ID cards. Expand accountable community policing. Enact strict gun controls. Embed restorative justice. Tackle hate crime, violence against women, and disability discrimination.

- Democracy: Renew local government with stronger powers, PR for councils and Westminster, referenda and recall; elected House of Lords; a written constitution, disestablishment of the Church, and curbed royal powers. Devolve regionally; enhance Scottish/Welsh powers. Oppose an undemocratic EU constitution while pursuing EU reform.

- Peace and international policy: Pursue an ethical foreign policy; oppose the Iraq war, replace UK troops with UN peacekeepers. Cut defence to the EU average; end arms export subsidies; back an Arms Trade Treaty; decommission nuclear weapons. Raise aid to at least 1% of GNI; cancel debts of the 52 poorest countries; support a Tobin tax. Reform the UN (end permanent Security Council seats) and democratise IMF/World Bank. Replace/transform WTO rules with a General Agreement on Sustainable Trade favouring localisation, fairness and environmental limits. Uphold asylum rights: benefits, right to work, independent appeals; ratify migrant and refugee conventions.

Judge whether TEXT_E or TEXT_C aligns more closely with this profile, taking into account that each foundation may be invoked in either direction.

Respond with a single JSON object and nothing else. Do not wrap it in markdown code fences and do not add commentary before or after it. The object must have exactly these keys, in this order:

{
  "evidence": "<the specific commitments in each text you relied on>",
  "reasoning": "<two sentences connecting that evidence to the verdict>",
  "confidence": "high" | "medium" | "low",
  "winner": "TEXT_E" | "TEXT_C"
}
